summary: This informational document analyzes common security threats against the MANET Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) and their potential impacts on routing protocols that use it. It does not propose solutions.

eli5.summary: This lists how bad actors could mess with neighbors saying hello in a wireless group. It only lists problems and gives no fixes.

questions: what is identity spoofing in manet
subtitle: A catalogue of ways an attacker can poison the neighbor tables that MANET routing depends on.

tldr.problem: NHDP lets wireless ad hoc routers learn their 1-hop and 2-hop neighbors by exchanging HELLO messages, but it has no built-in protection for the integrity of what it learns.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the attacks (jamming, denial of service, eavesdropping, identity and link spoofing, replay, timing attacks and more) and traces how bad neighbor data harms protocols such as OLSRv2 and SMF.
tldr.outcome: It proposes no solutions. It points to RFC 7185 for integrity protection and lists future work. RFC 7985 updates this document.

facts.label: Attacks catalogued
facts.value: Jamming, DoS, eavesdropping, spoofing, replay, timing and more

today: RFC 7186 is an Informational document that has been updated by RFC 7985; it has not been obsoleted. It is a threat analysis and specifies no protocol.

sections.title: Why NHDP Needs a Threat Analysis
sections.content:
The Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP, RFC 6130) lets routers learn topology up to two hops away through periodic HELLO messages. Other protocols, such as OLSRv2 (RFC 7181) and Simplified Multicast Forwarding (SMF, RFC 6621), build on that 1-hop and 2-hop information.

NHDP is typically used over wireless links, where any compatible device in radio range can hear and send. NHDP defines no explicit security measures for the integrity of what it learns. This document assumes no extra mechanism such as IPsec is used at the IP layer, because some MANET routers have limited resources. It analyses attacks and misconfigurations and what they do to the state each router keeps. It does not propose solutions.
sections.eli5: Neighbors in a wireless group learn who is close by listening to each other. Because anyone nearby can talk, a liar could trick them, so this paper studies the lies.

sections.title: Terms and the Threat Model
sections.content:
An attacker is a device in the network that intentionally tries to compromise the information bases in NHDP routers. A compromised NHDP router is an attacker that generates syntactically correct NHDP control messages, which may add or omit information compared to a legitimate router in the same position.

NHDP routers send HELLO messages by link-local multicast on each interface with a hop limit of 1, so HELLOs are never forwarded. In them a router announces addresses as heard, symmetric or lost neighbors. An attacker can announce wrong information about its identity, postulate nonexistent links, or replay HELLOs. The result can be inconsistent information bases that do not reflect the real topology, so protocols on top compute wrong paths or degrade flooding.
sections.eli5: A bad router is one that sends perfectly formed hellos that contain fibs. Hellos only travel one step, so each router only hears from its direct neighbors.

sections.title: The Catalogue of Attacks
sections.content:
Section 4 of the RFC describes each threat and maps it to the threat consequences of RFC 4593.

  • Jamming: massive interfering transmissions. If enough HELLOs are lost to collisions, NHDP presents empty information bases.
  • Denial of service: from misconfiguration (for example a very short HELLO interval) or a compromised router. Spoofed addresses can fill the Link and Neighbor Sets, huge 2-hop Sets can overflow memory, and battery-powered routers can be drained.
  • Eavesdropping and traffic analysis: passive, so it does not alter NHDP state, but it reveals topology. Traffic analysis can still work on encrypted HELLOs, using triggered HELLOs and message size.
  • Identity spoofing: using an address that is not the router's own in an address block, associated with a LOCAL_IF Address Block TLV.
  • Link spoofing: advertising neighbors that are not present, or leaving out real ones.
  • Replay: recording control traffic and replaying it elsewhere or later, for example by two colluding routers tunnelling HELLOs. Integrity checks cannot help because the original Integrity Check Value was correctly calculated.
  • Timing attacks: a spoofed HELLO with a low interval time can make a link look unreliable, and one with a low validity time (for example 1 ms) tears the link down.
  • Indirect channel overloading: the attacker alternately advertises a link as symmetric and lost so legitimate routers keep sending triggered HELLOs.
  • Attack on link quality update: spoofed packets that skip sequence numbers can lower link quality until the neighbor is removed (below HYST_REJECT).
sections.eli5: A trickster can shout over everyone, flood a router with fake friends, eavesdrop, pretend to be someone else, invent or hide friendships, repeat old messages, or lie about how long a message is good for.

sections.title: Damage to Routing and Flooding
sections.content:
Section 5 shows how a wrong neighbor table hurts protocols that use NHDP, mainly OLSRv2 and SMF.

MPR calculation. Multipoint relay (MPR) selection assumes that 1-hop and 2-hop information is accurate. A spoofed identity can make a legitimate relay look redundant, so a part of the network stops receiving flooded traffic. Spoofed links can make the compromised router the most appealing MPR, so it receives and is expected to relay all flooded traffic, which it can drop or manipulate. A broadcast storm results if a router is forced to select all its 1-hop neighbors as MPRs, degrading optimized flooding to classical flooding.

Other effects. Inconsistent information can cause routing loops (the examples show a loop between two routers), invalid or nonexistent paths to destinations, and a data sinkhole, where traffic for a spoofed identity is sent to the compromised router instead of the real destination.
sections.eli5: If the neighbor list is wrong, messages can get stuck going in circles, never reach part of the group, or be handed to the trickster, who can throw them away.

sections.title: Future Work and Mitigations Mentioned
sections.content:
The RFC says it does not propose solutions, but Section 6 suggests where new work could help. RFC 7185 specifies Integrity Check Values on HELLO messages, which gives an admittance mechanism for routers. The RFC notes that this creates a new DoS vector, since verifying an ICV needs CPU and memory, and that it does not address compromised routers.

  • Jamming: raise link metrics for jammed links so routing goes around.
  • Eavesdropping: ICVs are not encryption, so control traffic can still be read. Encrypting for a possibly undetermined set of neighbors is nontrivial.
  • Link spoofing: a router must still trust that the advertised links are right.
  • Replay: time synchronization between routers, or nonces instead of timestamps, could help.

For identity spoofing, timing attacks, indirect channel overloading and link quality attacks, RFC 7185 provides protection assuming the routers are not compromised.
sections.eli5: The authors do not fix anything here. They say where a lock on the messages could help, and where a lock is not enough because the liar is already inside the group.

viz.caption: SOME OF THE THREATS IN RFC 7186

items.title: Identity spoofing
items.text: A router claims an address that is not its own.

items.title: Link spoofing
items.text: Nonexistent neighbors are advertised, or real ones hidden.

items.title: Replay
items.text: Valid HELLOs are recorded and replayed elsewhere or later.

items.title: Timing attacks
items.text: Low interval or validity times make links look dead.
